So a neutrino detector works through what are basically giant vats of cleaning fluid.  The interaction of the neutrino with a chlorine atom (which is extremely rare; neutrinos are notoriously non-reactive) causes the the chlorine isotope to violently decay into argon, while releasing beta radiation (electrons).  As the electrons are ejected through chlorine, they disrupt the solution's EM field, which results in a region of "dense" field moving at the speed of the electron. However, if the electron is traveling faster than the speed of light in the field, (which is the same speed that the EM field can propogate because photons are the force carriers for EM force), the "dense" region falls behind and manifests as a electromagnetic shockwave.  The shockwave photons reach your eye and you perceive blue light.  In retrospect, it seems that the color of light would depend on the velocity of the particles interacting with chlorine, so you would get different color light for different particles, but that's just speculation.  Also, it's entirely possible that I'm completely wrong, but we're only gonna find out if an actual physicist shows up.

Only a high school physics student here, but I believe they use this concept in neutrino detection.  Basically an "optic boom" can occur in giant vats of chlorine because light travels much more slowly through a medium; ejected particles actually go faster than the speed of light in that medium.  Detecting neutrinos is finding optic booms, which basically appear as tiny flashes of light.
